Artificial intelligence searches vast design spaces, learns predictive models where first principles are intractable, and proposes unexpected candidate solutions. Applying these capabilities to computer systems and silicon chip design presents an unusually demanding test. An architectural decision begins with high-level workload intent and propagates through software runtimes, ISAs, microarchitectures, RTL, and physical silicon signoff. Measurements are expensive and inherently partial: simulators, compilers, formal models, synthesis reports, and post-layout analyses each reveal a different slice of the system under distinct operating assumptions. Verification must prove far more than whether a candidate design looks plausible, since a logic bug discovered after tapeout carries catastrophic financial and schedule costs.

That difficulty defines the opportunity. An *AI-native design system* rebuilds the design workflow so that learned methods, conventional simulators, and physical signoff tools operate as one system on a shared project representation, designing hardware and software together. The danger arrives with the capability: generators can produce candidates far faster than teams can evaluate them, and rapid generation helps only when the engineering process can verify what those candidates achieve.

This book investigates that transition with engineering discipline. The ambition extends beyond generating RTL from a prompt or training a standalone performance predictor. It asks whether a complete, closed-loop approach can produce superior architectures, reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable result, or achieve both. It does not assume this moonshot is solved; it establishes the principles and tool harnesses required to pursue it rigorously without confusing local progress with full-system success.

The architecture problem always comes first. Depending on the problem, the right approach may combine generation, prediction, optimization, conventional analysis, or no AI at all. Architecture 2.0 is not a claim that every design task requires machine learning; it is a framework to determine where AI earns its place and what evidence its use must produce.

## On the Title of This Book {.unnumbered}

The title of this book, *Architecture 2.0: Principles of AI-Native System and Chip Design*, is a compact statement of its scope, and each of its terms is deliberate.

Architecture 2.0 names a paradigm shift,[^fn-paradigm-shift-c00] which this book argues for rather than assumes, away from manual point-design sweeps toward autonomous, closed-loop exploration across the hardware-software stack. The book teaches *Principles* because its substance is the decision rules, evidence standards, and design trade-offs that architects face every day.

[^fn-paradigm-shift-c00]: **Author's note**: I do not use the term *paradigm shift* lightly. In the classic formulation of @Kuhn1962ScientificRevolutions, a paradigm shift occurs when a discipline's established methods encounter physical and operational limits that incremental improvements can no longer resolve. I argue that computer architecture has reached that condition, and this book supplies the evidence standard by which the claim should be judged. Independent use and later evidence will determine the verdict.

*AI-native* carries a precise engineering meaning here. Point AI assistance retrofits a model onto individual CAD tasks and leaves the surrounding process untouched. An AI-native design system instead builds the exploration workflow, machine-usable state representations, and verification harnesses around closed-loop search and multi-tool orchestration from the start. Finally, *System and Chip Design* reflects the physical reality that a silicon chip cannot be designed in isolation from the software compilers, memory hierarchies, interconnects, and physical signoff engines that surround it.

## What This Book Teaches {.unnumbered}

This book follows an architecture question through the engineering work required to answer it. As architects, we formulate the question and represent the design state, then select the methods and run the tools required to evaluate candidate solutions. What the tools return must be interpreted, compared against credible baselines, and turned into a technical recommendation that a human authority will own. This sequence keeps the focus on what architects must judge and execute rather than on any ephemeral model or tool.

When we evaluate whether adopting an automated workflow improves a design program, the object of study is the complete human-and-tool workflow. Candidate quality, final architecture performance, and the specific contribution of an AI model require separate, rigorous tests. A powerful model can sit inside a broken design loop, whereas a modest learned method can yield immense value if it eliminates the exact bottleneck constraining our decisions. The book condenses that discipline into two tests it applies throughout. Did the complete approach improve the work? And should anyone commit to the result? The first question is technical. The second one never is.

This book prepares an architect to master three foundational engineering competencies:

1. **State Representation and Method Selection:** Formulate precise architecture questions, expose cross-layer hardware-software dependencies in machine-usable representations, and select the smallest sufficient approach among conventional analysis, learned surrogates, generative synthesis, or optimization heuristics.
2. **Tool Execution and Physical Qualification:** Interface automated search loops to deterministic simulators, compilers, and signoff EDA engines via containerized harnesses, verifying that candidate improvements reflect genuine physical mechanisms rather than simulator proxy gaming.
3. **Rigorous Evaluation and Decision Ownership:** Measure complete-workflow gains against matched baselines at equal evaluation budgets, state remaining evidence limits plainly, and defend technical recommendations under human commitment authority.

To keep these principles concrete, this book uses a recurring Lighthouse case study featuring a real-time mobile extended reality compute subsystem under strict power and physical constraints. Nothing in that subsystem can be solved in isolation. The power envelope limits the accelerator, the accelerator reshapes memory traffic, and the memory hierarchy shifts thermal density across the die. The book returns to the Lighthouse at the points where the case exposes a fundamental principle, grounding the methods in executable reality rather than abstract claims. We subject this case study to the exact admission tests we establish for the field: where physical signoff decks, thermal extraction models, or matched baseline evidence are incomplete, the book records the outcome as unresolved rather than claiming an unearned tapeout victory.

Architecture 2.0 operates at the intersection of three established disciplines (@fig-book-composition).

![**Architecture 2.0 unifies computer architecture, machine learning, and EDA.** Computer architecture supplies the questions and design tradeoffs, machine learning supplies methods for learning and search, and EDA supplies executable implementation and analysis tools together with physical evidence or estimates. Work at their intersection must satisfy the relevant standards of all three.](images/fig-book-composition){#fig-book-composition width="100%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation, with Architecture 2.0 at their intersection"}

Operating at this intersection requires satisfying the evidence standards of all three fields simultaneously: simulation benchmarks from architecture and ML, physical signoff from architecture and EDA, and post-route metric fidelity from ML and EDA. A generated hardware block that ignores workload characteristics is not an architecture result; a learned estimate that fails physical signoff is not a physical result; and a successful tool run without a matched baseline comparison does not prove that AI improved the design.

To make this engineering scope precise, the book distinguishes three tiers of AI integration:

- **Point AI assistance (Tier 1)** accelerates an isolated task inside an established CAD flow (such as parameter tuning in a physical design engine or autocomplete in an RTL editor). These tools deliver immediate productivity within fixed layer boundaries, but they leave the broader architecture workflow and manual human integration unchanged.
- **AI-native design systems (Tier 2)** structure the entire cross-stack exploration workflow, machine-usable state representations, multi-tool orchestration, and verification harnesses around closed-loop search, carrying high-level system intent through physical qualification.
- **The Architecture Moonshot (Tier 3)** defines the program-level ambition that an AI-native design system can carry compact intent through real tools to physically realizable results under human commitment authority.

This book is not a catalog of current neural networks, a prompt-to-chip automation script, or a defense of using AI indiscriminately. It does not replace architectural judgment, compiler engineering, or formal verification with black-box models. Physical checks remain paramount, and named human architects remain answerable for the choices made and the silicon committed.

## Who This Book Is For {.unnumbered}

The primary audience is the practicing computer architect and systems researcher. This book assumes familiarity with performance, power, energy, area, and hardware-software interfaces, as well as the ability to evaluate architecture papers, simulator logs, and synthesis reports. It does not assume prior background in machine learning; it introduces all necessary ML concepts through concrete architecture problems and physical constraints.

Four technical communities meet at this intersection, each with distinct practical objectives:

- **Computer architects** seeking to integrate AI generation and search into rigorous design space exploration without losing control of physical constraints.
- **EDA and CAD engineers** looking to connect synthesis, placement, and verification tools to high-level architectural decision loops.
- **Machine learning and ML-systems researchers** entering hardware design who need to understand how physical signoff, evaluation costs, and formal verification redefine the criteria for a valid result.
- **Graduate students and engineering leaders** spanning hardware and software who want a shared vocabulary and rigorous framework for governing AI-native systems engineering.

## How to Read This Book {#book-structure .unnumbered}

While reading sequentially through all four parts provides the cumulative engineering argument, readers with specific technical priorities can also navigate via the modular pathways in @tbl-reading-pathways:

| Reader Persona | Primary Objective | Recommended Pathway | Key Anchor Chapters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hardware & Silicon Architects** | Integrate AI search without breaking physical constraints | Complete Sequential Path (Parts I $\rightarrow$ II $\rightarrow$ III $\rightarrow$ IV) | @sec-moonshot, @sec-architecture-20-ontology, @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-running-the-loop, @sec-what-architect-owns |
| **EDA & CAD Tool Developers** | Connect synthesis/layout engines to agentic exploration loops | Part II (Foundations) $\rightarrow$ Part III (Loops & Harnesses) | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, @sec-feedback-verification-trust, @sec-running-the-loop |
| **ML & ML-Systems Researchers** | Understand physical verification and matched-budget baselines | Part I $\rightarrow$ Part II (Methods & Verification) $\rightarrow$ Part III (Evaluation) | @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization, @sec-feedback-verification-trust, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect |
| **Engineering Directors & Executives** | Total-cost accounting, risk governance, and commitment ownership | Part I (Intent) $\rightarrow$ Part III (Evaluation & Ownership) $\rightarrow$ Part IV | @sec-moonshot, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, @sec-what-architect-owns, @sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem |
: **Recommended modular reading pathways tailored to technical backgrounds.** Readers can choose between complete sequential progression across all four parts or targeted chapter tracks focused on physical constraints, tool harness construction, evaluation methodology, or engineering governance. {#tbl-reading-pathways}

Test these principles against a live design problem while reading. Ask what decision truly matters, what hidden constraints must be exposed, which baseline comparison is fair, what the tools actually measured, and what risks remain unverified. The measure of this book is whether its principles carry to design problems it never mentions.

Specific AI models, benchmark scores, and CAD tool interfaces will keep changing. The core reasoning in this book is built to outlast them. When we ground the work in problem formulation, state representation, tool discipline, rigorous evaluation, and human commitment authority, we can swap out every model and tool named here without losing the underlying architectural framework.

I expect AI to reshape how we design systems and chips, and I have tried to write the book that takes that possibility seriously without taking it on faith. Candidate generation alone will not drive the change. The future of our discipline belongs to design systems that connect high-level intent to verifiable physical evidence, and to architects with the judgment to govern them. Architecture 2.0 is the disciplined foundation for deciding where AI belongs, where it does not, and what the evidence proves.
